question.text: Unpolarized light of intensity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn mathvariant="italic">I</mn></math> passes through an ideal polariser <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math>. Another identical polariser <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math> is placed behind <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math>. The intensity of light beyond B is found to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn mathvariant="italic">I</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>. Now another identical polariser <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>C</mi></math> is placed between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math>. The intensity beyond B is now found to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn mathvariant="italic">I</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></math> . The angle between polariser <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>C</mi></math> is

solution.text:
Transformation axis A and B are parallel. If the transformation axis of C is making angle θ with A, it will make angle 90−θ with B. Therefore,

⇒I2cos2θcos2(90−θ)=I8⇒14sin22θ=14
